stories.summary: Tackling a seemingly insurmountable problem, Clemson University automotive engineering graduate students have designed and built a solar-powered electric vehicle that produces more energy than it consumes in the latest iteration of the university’s Deep Orange program. Deep Orange 17, dubbed the Luminetta, was unveiled Aug. 6 at the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research.

Developed in collaboration with BMW North America, Deep Orange 17 was inspired by a simple, if daunting, challenge from BMW researchers: build a vehicle that generates more energy than it consumes during everyday driving. stories.summary: As Wade Robbins and his crew of three tighten a large fishing net below Barkley Dam in far western Kentucky, they are capturing thousands of Asian carp above and below the water’s surface. The invasive species is notorious for its jumping. Soon, a barrage of Asian carp from the top of the net start to launch themselves out of the net – slamming into the boat’s deck and hitting nearby crew members.

Robbins’ crew regularly harvests thousands of carp using a large net known as a seine to circle and trap large schools of the infamous fish gathered around Barkley Dam’s areas of flowing water. Using the power of persuasion, KSB convinced businesses to replace many of the worst signs with more tasteful ones. In 1974 KSB created an “Outline for Business Signs” with voluntary suggestions for businesses, followed in 1977 by a more formal “Guidelines for Effective Signs in the Sedona Area,” and in 1979 by “Guidelines for Architectural Designs.” That advocacy earned KSB a certificate of appreciation from the Governor’s Commission on Arizona’s Environment in 1981. stories.title: Stanford is running 37,000 AI agents as a virtual biotech — and one of its drug designs got independently confirmed by Merck
stories.summary: Stanford is running 37,000 AI agents as a virtual biotech — and one of its drug designs just got independently confirmed by Merck. The AI-powered lab designed new nanobody proteins for COVID variants that outperform human-designed ones. This could change how we think about drug discovery speed and scale.
stories.extended_summary: Merck just confirmed a drug design that came not from a human scientist, but from 37,000 collaborating AI agents operating as a virtual biotech. Stanford's James Zou built this AI lab to mirror his real research group, complete with an AI professor and AI students. The virtual team designed nanobody proteins for recent COVID variants that work even better than previous human-designed ones. It's a glimpse into a future where thousands of agents work together to tackle big problems — and the results are already making a real-world impact.

stories.title: The Miracle League Offers Opportunities for Those With Disabilities
stories.summary: The Miracle League is giving athletes with disabilities a real shot at baseball — with fully inclusive, year-round play. After seeing a player hit a home run and embrace her parents, a Chester County man worked to bring the league home. Now, communities across the U.S. are building accessible fields.
stories.extended_summary: Jim Moore watched a woman with disabilities hit a home run at a Miracle League game — and as she rounded the bases, her parents ran onto the field to embrace her. Moore was so moved he brought the league to Chester County. The Miracle League offers fully inclusive baseball for people with disabilities, and it's grown to 350+ communities. It's a reminder that everyone deserves to play.

stories.title: This Jewish museum is lending art across America — with one condition
stories.summary: The Jewish Museum is lending its art to museums across America — on one condition: don't display it in a separate Judaica gallery. Instead, pieces like Torah finials and a marriage panel are being integrated into broader art collections. It's a quiet move to show Jewish culture as part of the global diaspora, not apart from it.
stories.extended_summary: Walk into the Cleveland Museum of Art and you'll now find a Jewish ritual spice container in the Korean art gallery and Torah finials in the Middle East hall. That's by design: the Jewish Museum is lending works to museums with little or no Jewish art, with the condition that they're displayed alongside other cultures. The goal, says director James Snyder, is to reflect how Jewish culture has always been shaped by engagement with the world. It's a creative way to make museums more inclusive.

stories.title: Vermont leads effort to make trails accessible for all abilities
stories.summary: Vermont is making sure everyone can enjoy the outdoors. The state's adaptive trail assessment program — now a national model — helps adapt existing trails and build new ones with adaptive mountain bikers in mind. Over 250 miles of trails have been assessed so far.
stories.extended_summary: Vermont Adaptive, the Vermont Mountain Bike Association, and the Kelly Brush Foundation have teamed up to assess over 250 miles of trails across the state, making them accessible for adaptive mountain bikers. What started as a small program is now a nationwide model for inclusive trail design. The assessments include input from adaptive athletes themselves, ensuring the trails work for real riders. It's a big step toward making the outdoors open to everyone.

stories.title: Wheels on the Bus: Strollers Now Given Space on Entire MTA Fleet
stories.summary: Good news for NYC families: the MTA is adding designated stroller spaces to its entire bus fleet by the end of the year. The move builds on a successful pilot and preserves wheelchair-priority seating up front. Parents can now bring open strollers on board without blocking the aisle.
stories.extended_summary: Nearly 6,000 MTA buses will soon have designated stroller areas, with flip-up seats to make room for kids on the go. The program, which started as a pilot on seven routes, expands after advocates worked to protect wheelchair-priority spaces. New York City Transit president Demetrius Crichlow noted that buses help families get to school, work, and first play dates. It's a simple change that makes the city more navigable for parents and kids.

stories.extended_summary: In 2024, when Jeremiah Treece was a high school senior in Montgomery, Alabama, he noticed that his city’s flag reflected the Confederacy and Jim Crow laws, so he set about trying to change it. It’s a daunting challenge to change a city’s flag, but Jeremiah said the seven stars in the current flag, adopted in 1952, represented the seven states of the Confederacy, and the gold wreath represented “honor and glory.” Montgomery, a two-time All-America City, is “the heart of the civil rights movement,” Jeremiah said, “and symbols like this symbolize what the city stands for, and I don’t think anyone would want to be in a city that stands for division.” Over the next two years, Jeremiah gathered over a thousand signatures in support of his initiative to change the flag, and, along the way, he wor

stories.title: ‘These are storied areas’
stories.summary: A community-led effort in Hawaii is using roadside signs to honor traditional ahupua'a land divisions. The signs mark historic boundaries that stretch from mountains to sea, helping people recognize the storied land they're passing through. Nearly a dozen signs have been installed so far.
stories.extended_summary: Drive through the Hilo Paliku area of Hawaii Island and you'll now see signs marking ahupua'a — traditional land divisions that Native Hawaiians designed to sustain communities. The Makahanaloa Fishing Association pushed for the signs, and the state DOT created an application process for more. Coordinator Wai Wichimai says saying the names of these places 'breathes a little more life into the ʻāina and the history of that place.' It's a simple way to keep indigenous knowledge visible.

stories.title: “I Can Put My Guard Down”: How Restoring Promise Is Changing Prison Culture
stories.summary: A prison unit in Idaho transformed from a hotbed of fights and drugs into 'Cornerstone Village,' where residents start each day with a circle, a word of the day, and shared goals. The Restoring Promise initiative has cut violent infractions by 73% and restrictive housing stays by 83%. The culture shift is real—and it's measurable.
stories.extended_summary: At Idaho State Correctional Institution, the gray-walled unit known for trouble is now a community called Cornerstone Village. Correctional Sergeant Admir Efendic went from high alert to greeting residents with handshakes and joining their morning circle. They share challenges, set goals, and follow a pledge built on 'unity, trust, and mutual respect.' The results speak for themselves: a 73% reduction in violent infractions and 83% fewer restrictive housing stays. It's proof that treating people with dignity changes outcomes.

stories.title: 2 Renovated Englewood Properties Welcome Homeowners Under City’s Rebuild Program
stories.summary: Two vacant buildings in Englewood are now homes, thanks to Chicago's Neighborhood Rebuild Program. First-time homeowner Abria Williams cut the ribbon on her new two-flat, saying the South Side neighborhood has been 'a total 180' from what she'd heard. The city program is creating affordable homeownership opportunities.
stories.extended_summary: Abria Williams found her first home in an unexpected place: Englewood, which TikTok videos called the 'new hot spot.' She moved from the West Side and cut the ribbon on her renovated two-flat, one of two properties brought back to life through the city's Neighborhood Rebuild Program. The buildings were rehabbed by a Latino-owned business, attracting local economic development. For Williams, it's a fresh start and a chance to be part of the community's resurgence.

stories.title: California Expands Lunch Program That Pairs Schools With Farms
stories.summary: California just made its Farm to School program permanent, and kids are actually asking for seconds on salad. The program connects 500 school districts with local farmers, bringing fresh food like rambutan and pozole to lunch lines. One middle-schooler says he's never heard anyone complain about the food.
stories.extended_summary: In Lake Tahoe schools, students line up for rambutan and beg for more pozole. That's the kind of feedback that comes from California's Farm to School program, which pairs districts with local farms. The program was so successful that the state just made it permanent under the Department of Food and Agriculture. For nutrition directors like Christina Lawson, it's a relief after years of worrying about funding dry up. Soggy hot dogs and frozen pizza are getting replaced by fresh, locally sourced meals — and kids notice.

stories.title: Indiana Pilots New Path from Encampments to Housing
stories.summary: Indiana is testing a new model to move people from encampments to stable housing in just 4-6 weeks. 'Streets to Stability' pairs housing with rental subsidies, case management, and landlord incentives. In Indianapolis, a sister program has already housed 200 people, with 95% staying housed.
stories.extended_summary: Bloomington is launching 'Streets to Stability,' a program that helps people living in encampments transition to long-term housing within about a month. Each person gets a year of rental subsidy and individualized support, while landlords are incentivized to relax rules that often block people from being housed. The approach is modeled on Indianapolis's 'Streets to Home Indy,' which has housed 200 people and decommissioned seven encampments, with 95% still housed. It's a promising blueprint for ending chronic homelessness.

stories.extended_summary: In 2022, the longest “predator exclusion fence” anywhere in the Pacific was completed on Kauai, encircling 168 acres of prime seabird nesting habitat. stories.extended_summary: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed an artificial intelligence system designed to make autism screening faster and more objective for children.
